Existing Persistent Disks cannot be converted to CMEK in place, so noncompliant volumes must be replaced or migrated. • Grant the Compute Engine service agent for the cluster project roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the approved Cloud KMS key. • Create a new CMEK protected StorageClass using the Persistent Disk CSI driver, pd.csi.storage.gke.io, and the approved disk-encryption-kms-key value. • Update new PersistentVolumeClaims to use the CMEK protected StorageClass. If this should be the default storage option, mark the CMEK protected StorageClass as the default only after validating the key, location, and access permissions.

title: Use CMEK protected boot disks for GKE node pools
description: Use CMEK protected boot disks for GKE node pools so node boot disks are encrypted with approved Cloud KMS keys managed by the organization. This applies when creating a new cluster or creating a new node pool with the --boot-disk-kms-key setting. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project). Every node pool is checked.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.9.2 Use CMEK protected boot disks for GKE node pools

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container node-pools list --cluster "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(name,config.bootDiskKmsKey)') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F '\t' 'NF && !($2!="") {print $1 ": " $2}')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad"; fi

remediation.command: CMEK for node boot disks cannot be enabled, changed, or disabled in place for an existing node pool. To remediate a noncompliant node pool, create a replacement node pool with the approved Cloud KMS key, migrate workloads to the new node pool, validate workload health, and delete the old node pool after migration. Before creating the replacement node pool, grant the required Cloud KMS key access to the Compute Engine service agent for the cluster project. Create the replacement node pool with the approved boot disk type and Cloud KMS key. Current GKE CMEK boot disk guidance uses pd-standard or pd-ssd for this configuration.

title: Enforce image provenance using Binary Authorization for GKE
description: Use Binary Authorization for GKE to enforce image provenance and deploy time trust policies before container images are admitted to the cluster. Policies should allow only approved images, trusted registries, or images with required attestations from approved build, security, or release processes. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.5.1 Enforce image provenance using Binary Authorization for GKE

audit.command: Review the GKE Standard cluster and confirm that Binary Authorization enforcement is enabled and confirm it does not simply allow all images and that it requires approved images, trusted registries, or attestations from trusted attestors where appropriate. Binary Authorization works with Standard clusters and evaluates the configured policy at deploy time.

remediation.command: Enable Binary Authorization enforcement for the GKE Standard cluster and configure the policy to block unapproved images at deploy time. Use approved image rules, trusted registries, or attestation based requirements aligned to the build, security scan, and release approval process. Validate the policy in dry run or a lower environment before enforcing broadly in production.

title: Require RuntimeDefault seccomp or approved custom profiles for workload pods
description: Require GKE workload pods to use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile unless an approved custom Localhost profile is required. Seccomp should be configured in the pod or container security context to reduce the system calls available to containers. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.2 Require RuntimeDefault seccomp or approved custom profiles for workload pods

audit.command: Review running Pods across all namespaces and identify containers that do not explicitly use RuntimeDefault or an approved Localhost seccomp profile. In GKE Standard clusters, seccomp must be applied manually because GKE does not apply a profile for you. echo -e "NAMESPACE\tPOD\tCONTAINER\tEFFECTIVE_SECCOMP" kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r ' .items[] as $p | ($p.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type // "unset") as $podProfile | (($p.spec.containers // []) + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] | (.securityContext.seccompProfile.type // $podProfile) as $effective | ...

remediation.command: Update the workload controller templates for any Pods returned by the audit so seccomp is defined in the source manifest, not patched directly on running Pods. Apply the setting through the owning Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob, Helm chart, Kustomize overlay, or GitOps source. • Set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to RuntimeDefault at the Pod level where possible so all containers inherit the runtime default seccomp profile. • Use container level seccomp settings only when a specific container requires a different approved profile than the rest of the Pod. • Replace Unconfined with RuntimeDefault unless there is a documented and approved exception. • Allow Localhost only for approved custom seccomp profiles, and confirm the profile is documented, tested, and available on every node where the workload can run.

title: Require hardened security contexts for all workload Pods and containers
description: Require hardened security contexts for GKE workload Pods and containers. Security contexts should define workload level and container level controls that reduce privilege, limit host exposure, and enforce safer runtime behavior. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.3 Require hardened security contexts for all workload Pods and containers

audit.command: Review workload Pods and controller templates to confirm hardened security contexts are explicitly defined at the Pod and container level. Focus the audit on workload namespaces and verify settings such as runAsNonRoot=true, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, privileged=false, dropped Linux capabilities where practical, and seccompProfile.type=RuntimeDefault or an approved custom profile. GKE Standard supports using Pod Security Admission, Policy Controller, and security posture scanning to identify and enforce workload configuration risks.

remediation.command: Update workload manifests, Helm charts, overlays, or GitOps sources so hardened security contexts are defined before deployment. Apply settings at the Pod level when they apply to all containers, and use container level settings where a specific container requires a different configuration. • Set workloads to run as non root where compatible. • Set allowPrivilegeEscalation=false for workload containers. • Set privileged=false and remove host level access unless explicitly required. • Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, and use drop: ["ALL"] where the application supports it. • Set seccompProfile.type=RuntimeDefault or use an approved custom Localhost profile. Redeploy the workload and validate application behavior in a lower environment before broad rollout.

title: Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace
description: Avoid deploying GKE workloads in the default namespace. Use dedicated namespaces to separate applications, environments, or tenants so namespace level controls can be applied consistently. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 4.6.4 Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace

audit.command: Run the following command to identify resources currently deployed in the default namespace: kubectl get all,configmaps,secrets,pvc,ingress,serviceaccounts,networkpolicies -n default Review any returned resources and determine whether they are application, environment, or tenant workloads that should be moved to a dedicated namespace. GKE supports identifying workloads running in the default namespace and migrating them to dedicated namespaces to improve reliability and security.

remediation.command: Create dedicated namespaces for workloads based on application, environment, or tenant boundaries, then migrate application resources out of the default namespace. Make updates so all workload resources explicitly specify the new target namespace. After migration, apply appropriate namespace level governance, including RBAC, ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, Pod Security labels, and ownership labels.

title: Use COS_CONTAINERD node images for GKE node pools
description: Use COS_CONTAINERD node images for GKE node pools unless there is a specific workload requirement for Ubuntu or Windows. COS_CONTAINERD provides Container-Optimized OS with containerd, giving GKE nodes a Google maintained operating system image that is built, optimized, and hardened for running containers. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project). Every node pool is checked.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.5.1 Use COS_CONTAINERD node images for GKE node pools

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container node-pools list --cluster "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(name,config.imageType)') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F '\t' 'NF && !(toupper($2)=="COS_CONTAINERD") {print $1 ": " $2}')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad"; fi

remediation.command: Update noncompliant GKE node pools to use COS_CONTAINERD unless there is a documented requirement for Ubuntu or Windows node images. This remediation changes the node image for the selected node pool and should be planned as a node pool upgrade activity. gcloud container clusters upgrade $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=$LOCATION \ --project=$PROJECT_ID \ --node-pool=$NODE_POOL \ --image-type=COS_CONTAINERD After the upgrade completes, rerun the audit command and verify that the node pool reports COS_CONTAINERD. Validate workloads before and after the change, especially anything that depends on host level packages, Ubuntu specific behavior, Windows nodes, or Docker Engine access.

title: Verify node auto-repair is enabled for GKE node pools
description: Verify node auto-repair is enabled for GKE node pools so unhealthy nodes are automatically repaired and returned to a healthy running state. Node auto-repair is enabled by default for new node pools, but for older node pools should still be reviewed for compliance. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project). Every node pool is checked.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.5.2 Verify node auto-repair is enabled for GKE node pools

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container node-pools list --cluster "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(name,management.autoRepair)') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F '\t' 'NF && !($2=="True") {print $1 ": " $2}')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad"; fi

remediation.command: Enable node auto-repair for any GKE node pool where the audit result is not true. This allows GKE to monitor nodes in the node pool and automatically repair nodes that fail health checks for an extended period. gcloud container node-pools update $POOL_NAME \ --cluster=$CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=$LOCATION \ --project=$PROJECT_ID \ --enable-autorepair After remediation, rerun the audit command and confirm that management.autoRepair returns true. If multiple node pools are present, repeat the audit and remediation for each applicable node pool.

title: Verify node auto-upgrade is enabled for GKE node pools
description: Verify node auto-upgrade is enabled for GKE node pools so nodes receive supported Kubernetes versions, node image updates, and security fixes through the managed upgrade process. Node auto-upgrade is enabled by default for new GKE node pools, but it should still be reviewed for older node pools. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project). Every node pool is checked.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.5.3 Verify node auto-upgrade is enabled for GKE node pools

audit.command:
out=$(gcloud container node-pools list --cluster "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(name,management.autoUpgrade)') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk -F '\t' 'NF && !($2=="True") {print $1 ": " $2}')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad"; fi

remediation.command: Enable node auto-upgrade for any GKE node pool where the audit result is not true. This allows GKE to automatically schedule eligible node pools for upgrades when upgrade targets become available, subject to maintenance windows, maintenance exclusions, release channel behavior, and upgrade rollout constraints. gcloud container node-pools update $POOL_NAME \ --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --enable-autoupgrade After remediation, rerun the audit command and confirm that management.autoUpgrade returns true. If multiple node pools are present, repeat the audit and remediation for each applicable node pool.

title: Enroll GKE clusters in release channels for automated version management
description: Enroll GKE clusters in an appropriate release channel to automate version management and align cluster upgrades with the organization’s required balance of feature availability, upgrade predictability, and production stability. Release channels let teams choose how quickly clusters receive supported Kubernetes versions, patches, security fixes, and GKE updates without manually selecting every version. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.5.4 Enroll GKE clusters in release channels for automated version management

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(releaseChannel.channel)') || exit 1
if case "$v" in REGULAR|STABLE) true;; *) false;; esac; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: releaseChannel.channel=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Enroll the existing GKE cluster in an approved release channel rather than recreating the cluster. Use regular or stable unless the organization has approved another channel for a documented use case. Before changing the release channel, confirm that the cluster control plane version is available in the target channel and configure maintenance windows or exclusions if upgrade timing needs to be controlled. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=$LOCATION \ --project=$PROJECT_ID \ --release-channel=$RELEASE_CHANNEL After remediation, rerun the audit command and verify that .releaseChannel.channel returns the approved channel. For clusters enrolled in a release channel, node auto-upgrade is managed as part of the GKE release channel upgrade process, so maintenance policies should be reviewed to reduce workload disruption during automatic upgrades.

title: Do not use GKE alpha clusters for production workloads
description: Do not use GKE alpha clusters for production workloads. Alpha clusters are intended only for short lived testing of Kubernetes alpha APIs and features, and they are not covered by the GKE SLA. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.10.1 Do not use GKE alpha clusters for production workloads

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(enableKubernetesAlpha)') || exit 1
if [ "$v" != True ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: enableKubernetesAlpha=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Alpha cluster behavior is selected at cluster creation and should not be used for production workloads. To remediate a production workload running on an alpha cluster, create a supported non alpha GKE cluster, migrate workloads and required data, validate application health, and decommission the alpha cluster. Alpha clusters expire after 30 days, do not receive security updates, cannot be upgraded, and are not covered by the GKE SLA. gcloud container clusters create $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID Do not include the --enable-kubernetes-alpha flag when creating the replacement production cluster. If alpha features are needed for testing, use a separate nonproduction alpha cluster and migrate any required data before the 30 day expiration window.

title: Use GKE Sandbox for untrusted or high risk workloads
description: Use GKE Sandbox for untrusted, third party, multi tenant, or high risk workloads that need stronger isolation from the node host. GKE Sandbox uses gVisor to add an isolation layer between the container and the host kernel, reducing the risk that untrusted code can affect the node. Reported as a manual review because it needs site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.10.2 Use GKE Sandbox for untrusted or high risk workloads

audit.command: Review the GKE node pool and verify that GKE Sandbox is enabled for node pools that run untrusted or high risk workloads. GKE Sandbox uses gVisor to provide additional isolation between the container and the host kernel. gcloud container node-pools describe $NODE_POOL \ --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --format json | jq '.config.sandboxConfig' • Expected result: the output should show the sandbox type as GVISOR. The older sandboxType field can appear in some output, but the current field is type.

remediation.command: Create a new GKE Sandbox enabled node pool for untrusted or high risk workloads. GKE Sandbox cannot be enabled on the default node pool when it is the only node pool, and GKE Sandbox node pools must use the cos_containerd node image. gcloud container node-pools create $NODE_POOL \ --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --image-type=cos_containerd \ --sandbox type=gvisor Update workload manifests for untrusted or high risk workloads to request the gvisor RuntimeClass. spec: runtimeClassName: gvisor Migrate the applicable workloads to the sandbox enabled node pool, validate application behavior, and confirm the Pods are running with runtimeClassName: gvisor. Keep trusted system workloads and regular workloads on separate node pools unless there is an approved reason to run them in the sandbox.

title: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for cluster security insights
description: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard to surface cluster and workload security insights, including workload configuration auditing, actionable security concerns, and security bulletin related findings. The dashboard provides a centralized view of security posture findings so teams can identify, prioritize, and remediate issues across eligible GKE clusters and workloads. Requires gcloud with container.clusters.get; the cluster comes from GKE_CLUSTER and GKE_LOCATION (optional GKE_PROJECT, else the gcloud default project).
reference: CIS Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Benchmark v2.0.0 - 5.10.3 Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for cluster security insights

audit.command:
v=$(gcloud container clusters describe "${GKE_CLUSTER:?set GKE_CLUSTER}" --location "${GKE_LOCATION:?set GKE_LOCATION}" ${GKE_PROJECT:+--project=$GKE_PROJECT} --format='value(securityPostureConfig.mode)') || exit 1
if case "$v" in BASIC|ENTERPRISE) true;; *) false;; esac; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: securityPostureConfig.mode=$v"; fi

remediation.command: Enable the GKE security posture dashboard for workload configuration auditing when the audit shows that securityPostureConfig.mode is not BASIC. GKE supports enabling configuration auditing on existing clusters by setting the security posture mode to standard, which maps to BASIC in the cluster configuration. gcloud container clusters update $CLUSTER_NAME \ --location $LOCATION \ --project $PROJECT_ID \ --security-posture=standard For new clusters, include --security-posture=standard during cluster creation when this setting must be explicitly enforced. Rerun the audit command and confirm that securityPostureConfig.mode returns BASIC. Initial configuration audit results can take several minutes to appear in the security posture dashboard and related logs.
